headings.title: Introduction and Definition of the Diaphragm
headings.content: The diaphragm is a dome-shaped, shallow silicone or latex cup with a flexible, springy rim designed to act as a barrier method of contraception. For nursing students preparing for clinical practice and board examinations in Nigeria, understanding the anatomical placement and barrier function of the diaphragm is vital. The device is inserted vaginally prior to coitus so that it rests snugly in the vaginal vault, completely covering the external cervical os. By positioning itself over the cervix, the diaphragm physically prevents spermatozoa from ascending into the upper reproductive tract, thereby blocking fertilization. To enhance its contraceptive efficacy, the diaphragm must always be used in conjunction with a chemical spermicide cream or jelly, which immobilizes and destroys sperm upon contact. While it does not protect against sexually transmitted infections (STIs), it offers a hormone-free alternative for individuals who wish to avoid the systemic side effects of hormonal contraceptives. Nursing professionals play a key role in explaining how this barrier method works, ensuring clients comprehend that dual protection is still necessary if STI prevention is a priority.

headings.title: Mechanism of Action in Family Planning
headings.content: The mechanism of action of the diaphragm relies on a dual-protection approach combining a physical barrier and a chemical agent. Mechanically, the dome of the device blocks sperm from entering the cervical canal and reaching the ovum. Chemically, the spermicide applied to the inner dome and rim of the diaphragm immobilizes sperm on contact, drastically reducing their motility and viability. Because sperm can swim rapidly through microscopic gaps, the combination of the snug-fitting silicone or latex dome and the spermicidal barrier creates a highly effective defense against unwanted pregnancy. For the mechanism to succeed, the diaphragm must remain in place for a specified minimum duration following intercourse—typically at least six hours—allowing adequate time for all trapped sperm to be rendered inactive by the spermicide. Nurses must educate clients that removing the diaphragm too early, before the six-hour window has elapsed, significantly increases the risk of fertilization as viable sperm may still be present in the vaginal canal.

headings.title: Types and Sizing of Diaphragms
headings.content: Diaphragms are manufactured in various types and sizes to accommodate individual pelvic anatomies. The primary types of rims include the coil spring, flat spring, and arcing spring diaphragms, each providing different levels of flexibility and ease of insertion. The coil spring features a soft, rounded spring suitable for women with normal pelvic muscle tone. The flat spring is similar but has a flatter rim, making it useful for women with a shallow pubic arch. The arcing spring diaphragm bends in a specific way, making it easier to insert and position correctly, and is generally considered the most versatile type. Sizing is critical and must be performed by a trained healthcare professional, such as a nurse or midwife, using a set of fitting rings. Sizes typically range from 50 mm to 95 mm, measured by the diameter of the rim. An improper size can lead to displacement during coitus, resulting in contraceptive failure, or can cause pelvic discomfort, pressure, or tissue irritation for the client.

headings.title: Indications, Contraindications, and Client Selection
headings.content: Client selection for a diaphragm requires a careful review of indications and contraindications to ensure safety and effectiveness. Indications include women seeking a non-hormonal, reversible method of birth control who have adequate pelvic muscle tone to support the device. Contraindications involve conditions such as a history of Toxic Shock Syndrome (TSS), known allergy to latex or silicone, severe uterine prolapse, cystocele, or rectocele that distorts normal vaginal anatomy, and frequent urinary tract infections. Additionally, women with poor pelvic floor muscle tone, postpartum clients whose uterus has not fully involuted (usually within the first 6 weeks postpartum), and women with anomalies of the vaginal tract are poor candidates. Nurses must conduct a thorough health history and physical assessment during family planning consultations. Identifying these risk factors early prevents complications and guides clients toward more suitable alternative contraceptive methods when a diaphragm is contraindicated.

headings.title: Nursing Assessment and Fitting Procedure
headings.content: The nursing assessment and fitting procedure require clinical skill, sensitivity, and patient education. The nurse begins by taking a comprehensive reproductive and medical history, followed by a pelvic examination to evaluate the health of the reproductive organs and assess pelvic floor muscle strength. Using a bimanual examination and a set of fitting rings, the nurse estimates the correct size of the diaphragm. The fitting ring should rest comfortably in the posterior vaginal fornix and behind the pubic symphysis without causing pressure or displacement when the client bears down. Once the correct size is determined, the nurse provides the client with a demonstration model to practice insertion and removal in the clinic. The nurse also assesses for re-fitting needs, which are mandatory after a weight fluctuation of 10 pounds or more, following a full-term pregnancy, or after any gynecological surgery, as these events alter pelvic dimensions.

headings.title: Client Education on Insertion, Removal, and Spermicide Use
headings.content: Comprehensive client education is essential for the successful use of a diaphragm. The nurse must teach the client how to inspect the device for pinholes or cracks by holding it up to the light or filling it with water. Before insertion, the client must apply about a tablespoon of spermicidal cream or jelly inside the dome and along the rim. To insert, the client squeezes the rim together and pushes the device deep into the vagina, ensuring the front rim tucks securely behind the pubic bone. The client should check with a finger to confirm that the cervix is covered by the dome. The diaphragm must be inserted no more than six hours before intercourse. If intercourse is repeated, additional spermicide must be applied vaginally without removing the device. For removal, the client hooks a finger over the rim, pulls downward and outward, and safely extracts it. Nurses must ensure the client can successfully perform these steps before leaving the clinic.

headings.title: Care, Maintenance, and Lifespan of the Device
headings.content: Proper care and maintenance maximize the lifespan of the diaphragm and protect the client from vaginal infections. After removal, the diaphragm should be washed thoroughly with mild soap and warm water, rinsed completely, and allowed to air dry completely. Clients must avoid using harsh chemical cleansers, abrasive soaps, or oil-based lubricants (such as petroleum jelly), as these substances break down latex and silicone materials, creating microscopic tears that compromise effectiveness. Once dry, the diaphragm should be stored in its provided clean, cool container away from direct sunlight and extreme heat. Talcum powder or cornstarch should not be applied to the device, as they can cause irritation. With proper care and regular inspection, a high-quality silicone or latex diaphragm can typically last between one to two years before it needs to be replaced. Nurses should reinforce these maintenance guidelines during routine follow-up visits.

headings.title: Advantages and Limitations of the Diaphragm
headings.content: The diaphragm presents a unique set of advantages and limitations that nursing students must understand to counsel clients effectively. Advantages include being non-hormonal, user-controlled, and reversible, making it ideal for women who cannot or prefer not to use hormonal contraceptives or intrauterine devices. It can be inserted ahead of time, does not permanently disrupt spontaneity when used skillfully, and offers some degree of barrier protection against certain upper reproductive tract infections. However, limitations include a relatively high typical-use failure rate compared to hormonal methods, largely due to user error such as incorrect placement or failing to use spermicide. It requires preparation prior to intercourse, may increase the risk of urinary tract infections due to pressure on the urethra from the rim, and demands a level of body awareness and comfort with touching one's genitalia that not all clients possess. Nursing counseling should weigh these pros and cons against the client's lifestyle and reproductive goals.

headings.title: Potential Complications and Troubleshooting
headings.content: Potential complications associated with diaphragm use must be recognized and managed promptly by healthcare professionals. One of the most serious, though rare, complications is Toxic Shock Syndrome (TSS), a severe systemic illness linked to prolonged retention of barrier devices and certain bacterial strains. Signs of TSS include sudden high fever, vomiting, diarrhea, a sunburn-like rash, dizziness, and muscle aches. Other common issues include recurrent urinary tract infections (UTIs) resulting from mechanical pressure of the rim on the urethra, allergic reactions to latex or spermicide (manifesting as vaginal itching, burning, or redness), and localized vaginal tissue irritation or abrasions. Nurses play a crucial troubleshooting role by advising clients to remove the diaphragm immediately if TSS symptoms appear, treating UTIs promptly, and recommending alternative materials (such as silicone instead of latex) or alternative spermicides if allergic contact dermatitis occurs.
